section: Educational Psychology · Ch8 — Bandura's 4 Stages of Observational Learning
subject: Educational Psychology
stem: According to Bandura, before a child can imitate a teacher's demonstration of cursive handwriting, the child must first:

options.option_text: Pay attention to and accurately perceive the model's demonstration
Already be able to perform the skill perfectly
Have no motivation of any kind

explanation: Attention is the first of Bandura's four stages of observational learning — without noticing and accurately perceiving the model's behaviour, no learning from observation can begin.

section: Educational Psychology · Ch8 — Bandura's 4 Stages of Observational Learning
subject: Educational Psychology
stem: A student watches a science demonstration on Monday and successfully repeats the procedure from memory on Friday, several days later. This delayed reproduction is possible because of Bandura's second stage:

options.option_text: Retention — mentally storing the observed behaviour as a symbolic representation
Attention only, with no memory storage involved
Motivation only, with no memory storage involved
Reproduction happening instantly with no delay ever possible

explanation: Retention involves encoding the observed behaviour into memory (often as mental images or verbal descriptions), enabling reproduction even after a significant time delay — this is what distinguishes observational learning from mere momentary mimicry.

section: Educational Psychology · Ch8 — Bandura's 4 Stages of Observational Learning
subject: Educational Psychology
stem: A student who has attended to and retained a demonstrated dance step, but lacks the physical coordination to perform it correctly, is failing at Bandura's stage of:

options.option_text: Reproduction — the physical/motor capability to actually perform the observed behaviour

explanation: Reproduction is the third stage — translating the retained mental representation into actual motor performance, which requires the physical capability to execute the behaviour, distinct from having merely noticed and remembered it.
